edits.before: Electroweak theory also predicted an associated particle called the <term>Higgs boson</term>. The mass of this particle is not predicted with nearly the certainty with which the mass of the <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mi>W</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">+</m:mo><m:mrow/></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:msup><m:mi>,</m:mi><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:msup><m:mi>W</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">−</m:mo><m:mrow/></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow><m:mo>,</m:mo></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> and <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mi>Z</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Z rSup { size 8{0} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> particles were predicted, but it was hoped that the Higgs boson could be observed at the now-canceled Superconducting Super Collider (SSC). In 2012, experiments at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN discovered a Higgs boson with a mass of approximately <m:math><m:mn>125</m:mn><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext>GeV</m:mtext><m:mo lspace="0" rspace="0">/</m:mo><m:msup><m:mi>c</m:mi><m:mn>2</m:mn></m:msup></m:math>. This discovery provided experimental support for the Higgs mechanism underlying electroweak symmetry breaking.
edits.after: Electroweak theory predicts a particle associated with the Higgs field, called the <term>Higgs boson</term>, but does not predict its mass. In 2012, the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider discovered this particle, with a mass of approximately <m:math><m:mn>125</m:mn><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext>GeV</m:mtext><m:mo lspace="0" rspace="0">/</m:mo><m:msup><m:mi>c</m:mi><m:mn>2</m:mn></m:msup></m:math>. The discovery supports the Higgs mechanism, through which the W and Z bosons acquire mass while the photon remains massless.
